newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch launch milk prodcution quota exchange.
newsitem.headline: Dutch launch milk prodcution quota exchange.

text.p: An exchange was launched in the Netherlands on Tuesday to facilitate trade in milk production quotas among the country's 30,000 dairy farmers.

The company running the exchange said it was modelled on the world's only other milk quota bourse in Canada, and it plans to attract quotas covering 10 percent of the Dutch national milk allocation of 11 billion tonnes.
Under the European Union's milk regime, each member state receives a national production quota, which is in turn divided up among its farmers.
The new bourse will allow farmers, who have exceeded their quota and would under normal circumstances face a fine for doing so, to buy a bigger allocation.
"The main aim is to provide greater transparency," Thijs Stoffer, spokesman for the Nationale Melk Quota Beurs (NMQB) told Reuters.
He said the initial focus would be on Dutch farmers, but the system was appropriate for wider international participation, and this may be considered in the future.

NMQB is not planning an electronic exchange but farmers interested in trading a quota are asked to telephone the bourse headquarters in the northern town of Leeuwarden. They will then be told what quotas are being offered by other farmers.
Stoffer said NMQB was also looking at using the internet to facilitate its activities and that agricultural real estate brokers may also be attracted to trade the market.

But there is a possible cloud on the horizon. The EU is looking to reform its elaborate milk quota regime, which has been criticised as being incompatible with world free trade rules and the bloc's proposed enlargement eastwards.
The 13-year old system is due to expire at end-March 2000.
"Some countries are looking to end the system of quotas but most expect some sort of system involving them will survive," Stoffer said.
EU farm ministers meeting in the Netherlands last month signalled there may only be a modest reform of the regime.
